extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of literary and political criticism (general 19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-critical essay evaluating the character, motives, style, and public conduct of prominent political figures. The page offers evaluative standards and illustrative examples for judging public men (e.g., Sir Francis Burdett, Lord Eldon, Mr Wilberforce, Mr Canning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry expands capability; indolence impoverishes mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “the more we do, the more we can do; the more busy we are, the more leisure we have... It is not incapacity, but indolence, indecision, want of imagination... that leaves us so poor, so dull, and inert as we are.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive sign: active pursuit of studies/profession, using spare time to cultivate faculties (examples: making a fortune, learning languages, taking the grand tour). Anti-pattern: habitual idleness, repetitive small routines (e.g., always sitting in same coffee-house, walking the same streets) that prevent acquisition and enlargement of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of experience enlarges views
rubrics_metrics.description: “...by employing his spare time and cultivating the waste faculties of his mind... Mr. Brougham... has visited, we believe, most of the courts, and turned his attention to most of the Constitutions of the continent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued: travel, comparative study, exposure to other institutions and cultures as means to strengthen and enlarge understanding. Example: studying foreign constitutions and courts as intellectual enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty in display of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is a plain, unaffected, unsophisticated English gentleman... he makes very little display of [his reading], unless it be to quote Shakespear, which he does often with extreme aptness and felicity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive trait: knowledge shown by apt use rather than ostentation. Guidance: modest use of learning (occasional apt quotation) preferred to continual display or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty, common sense, and humanity as core virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: “All that he pretends to is common sense and common honesty... his humanity is unconstrained and free. His heart does not ask leave of his head to feel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public figures by plain honesty and humane feeling; being listened to and admired by constituents can indicate these virtues. Example: letters to constituents noted as especially good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage to speak sincere convictions despite discomfort
rubrics_metrics.description: “We cannot conceive a higher proof of courage than the saying things which he has been known to say there; and we have seen him blush and appear ashamed of the truths he has been obliged to utter, like a bashful novice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courageous sign: willingness to state uncomfortable truths even when they provoke shame or personal embarrassment. This is framed as a higher proof of courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature vs indolent selfishness (distinguish genuine virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mere good-nature (or what passes in the world for such) is often no better than indolent selfishness... Their charity begins and ends at home... All their patience is confined to the accidents that befal others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: outward affability masking self-indulgence; unruffled calm that collapses when personally affected. Test: whether one’s benevolence extends beyond personal comfort and convenience; observe responses when directly provoked or inconvenienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality compromised by self-interest or personal concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by Lord Chancellor coming to his place “with the statement in his hand, fire in his eyes, and a direct charge of falsehood... without making any inquiry into it... on no better authority than a common newspaper report.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative sign: readiness to decide and condemn when one is personally touched, without inquiry or caution. Guidance: true impartiality is shown by the same scrupulous fairness whether or not the matter affects oneself; failure evidences passion/self-love overriding reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive scrupulousness/delay as a fault
rubrics_metrics.description: “He delights to balance a straw, to see a feather turn the scale... He hugs indecision to his breast, and takes home a modest doubt... Delay seems, in his mind, to be of the very essence of justice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While conscientious exactness is proverbially good, an overindulgence in nicety, quibbles, and protracted indecision can become tormenting and frustrate justice. Anti-pattern: preferring perpetual balancing to decisive resolution; preference for delay over timely justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/Immediate motives often prevail over abstract principle
rubrics_metrics.description: “The personal always prevails over the intellectual, where the latter is not backed by strong feeling and principle... where remote and speculative objects do not excite a predominant interest and passion, gross and immediate ones are sure to carry the day.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a person's public choices are driven by immediate self-interest, desire to please, or short-sighted temperament versus consistent attachment to abstract principles or public good. Warning: even well-disposed private men may become dangerous public characters if pliable to passions of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed allegiance to power/servility as a character flaw
rubrics_metrics.description: “He has gone the whole length of the most unpopular designs of Ministers... on the side of prerogative and power, and against every proposal for the advancement of freedom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative marker: consistent support for prerogative, opposition to reforms, and uncritical deference to authority; attributed to want of imagination, phlegmatic habit, and false complaisance. Use historical/policy positions (wars, penal laws, Catholic emancipation, slave trade stance) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of good parts — choose and act up to one leading character
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man must take his choice not only between virtue and vice, but between different virtues... It is best to choose and act up to some one leading character, as it is best to have some settled profession or regular pursuit in life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive advice: coherence and selectivity of character produce respectability; trying to embody incompatible virtues (or all virtues at once) leads to affectation, cant, and loss of self-respect. Evaluate whether a person’s virtues are in practical tension and how they prioritize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience influenced by desire for public approbation
rubrics_metrics.description: “His next... is to do what will be thought so by other people. He is always at a game... his 'conscience will not budge,' unless the world goes with it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure integrity by whether actions follow inner convictions regardless of popularity. Anti-pattern: seeking validation from ministers or society (e.g., craving Prime-Minister's toast) and adjusting moral stance to secure reputation or office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity constrained by safety and self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “His humanity will go all lengths that it can with safety and discretion: but it is not to be supposed that it should lose him his seat... He is anxious to do all the good he can without hurting himself or his fair fame.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine sacrifice from calculated benevolence; evaluate whether humanitarian action is accompanied by willingness to bear personal cost. Anti-pattern: philanthropy that never threatens status, favour, or worldly interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must be matched by substance (no mere ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Mr. Canning: “His reasoning is a tissue of glittering sophistry; his language is a cento of florid common-places... The matter is nothing; the only question is, how he shall express himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive criterion: originality, steady principles, and strong thought trump mere rhetorical polish. Anti-patterns: speeches that are artificial, showy, forced, 'hot-house' exotics—beautiful in colour but lacking stamina or truth; rhetorical ornament that masks vacuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of interest vs narrow specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is a mere House-of-Commons man... not even the man of the world — he has passed his life in making and learning to make speeches... There is no allusion in any of his speeches to anything passing out of the House.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a public figure’s outlook is parochial and confined to institutional practice or whether it reflects engagement with wider life, nature, and ordinary human concerns. Narrow, specialized experience often produces mannered, second-hand thought rather than original insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and sincerity of speaking style
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding Mr. Wilberforce: “His style of speaking is not quite parliamentary, it is halfway between that and evangelical... It winds, and undulates, and glides up and down on texts of Scriptures... like those birds of weak wing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether style suits context and substance. A hybrid or affected delivery (e.g., evangelical-parliamentary mixture) can signal lack of straightforwardness or undermine authority. Evaluate tone, cadence, and rhetorical devices for sincerity and fit to occasion.
